title: Reflection and its trade-offs
description: Understand how .NET reflection works, when it is useful, and what performance and security costs it carries.

data.text: Reflection is the ability of a program to inspect, modify, and invoke types and members at runtime. It is one of the most powerful features in .NET — and one of the most expensive. Frameworks like ASP.NET Core, Entity Framework Core, and JSON serializers all rely on reflection to discover types, map properties, and build pipelines. But in performance-sensitive code paths, reflection can silently dominate CPU time and generate significant garbage-collection pressure.

The key to using reflection well is knowing when it is the right tool and when a source generator, a compiled expression, or a manually written dispatcher would be faster. Reflection is not inherently bad — it is the absence of an alternative. Modern .NET provides alternatives that give you the flexibility of reflection without the runtime cost.

When you call `typeof(MyClass)`, the runtime returns a `Type` object backed by the assembly's metadata tables. The metadata is already loaded — the CLR parsed it when the assembly was loaded. Reflection reads those tables rather than performing expensive disk I/O. The expense comes from string-based lookups, boxing of value types, and the creation of temporary delegate objects. A single reflection-heavy loop can allocate thousands of small objects per millisecond.

data.title: Reading type metadata with reflection

data.text: `System.Reflection.Emit` lets you generate new types, methods, and assemblies at runtime. It is used by serializers, ORMs, and proxy generators to build fast, type-specific code paths without writing the code by hand. A common pattern is to generate a dynamic method that reads or writes properties directly, avoiding the string-based overhead of `PropertyInfo.GetValue` on every call.

data.title: Creating a dynamic getter with Reflection.Emit

data.text: Source generators shift reflection work from runtime to compile time. A source generator runs during compilation, inspects your code using the Roslyn compiler API, and produces additional C# source files that are compiled alongside your project. Because the generated code is compiled ahead of time, there is no runtime reflection cost — and no trimming risk, since the compiler sees the generated code as regular source.

data.title: Source generator producing a mapper
Reflection and Native AOT do not mix well
data.text: Native AOT and trimming analyze your code statically. If they cannot see a type being referenced directly, they assume it is unused and remove it. Reflection bypasses the compiler, so the linker cannot see the types you reference by name string. You must annotate your code with `DynamicDependency` or `RequiresUnreferencedCode`, or provide `rd.xml` files to preserve types. Always test Native AOT builds with full integration tests that exercise every reflection path.

data.title: Key takeaways
items: Reflection reads embedded assembly metadata; its cost comes from string lookups, boxing, and delegate allocations.
Reflection.Emit generates IL at runtime to produce fast, type-specific delegates on demand.
Source generators move reflection work to compile time, eliminating runtime cost and trimming risk.
Native AOT requires explicit preservation of reflection-accessed types or the linker will remove them.
